module.title: Unit 6: How Do They Do It?: Passive Voice Present & Past
module.objective: Mampu menjelaskan urutan kejadian dan cara melakukan sesuatu menggunakan kalimat pasif bentuk present dan past, serta menggunakan struktur 'have something done' dengan tepat

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Behind the Scenes of World-Famous Illusions
subModules.theme: How Do They Do It?: Passive Voice Present & Past
subModules.grammarFocus: Passive Voice (Present and Past), Causative Have
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Extreme Adjectives, Performance and Illusion Vocabulary

content.summary: Welcome to the reading sub-module for Unit 6. In this lesson, you will explore how famous magic tricks, stunts, and spectacles are produced behind the scenes. You will practice identifying the passive voice in present and past tenses, learn how to use extreme adjectives with absolute modifiers, and discover how sentences change focus when the action receiver becomes the subject.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present Passive (am/is/are + past participle), Past Passive (was/were + past participle), and the Causative structure (have something done).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Extreme adjectives such as freezing, hilarious, and fascinating, alongside performance vocabulary like illusionist, spectator, and performer.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning paragraphs for specific passive structures and skimming for general information about stagecraft and magic.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of texts explaining how illusionists perform famous stunts.
Locate specific details regarding past events using the past passive voice.
Recognize and apply grammar patterns featuring present and past passive verbs.
Distinguish between standard adjectives and extreme adjectives in descriptive reading passages.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you watch a spectacular magic trick on television, what do you usually wonder about first?
options: How the secret method is hidden from the audience.
What the performer ate for breakfast.
How much money the television station spent on cameras.
contextWarmup.explanation: When watching illusions, viewers naturally focus on how the secret is kept and how the trick is performed rather than unrelated trivial details.

rules: Present Passive is formed using Subject + am/is/are + past participle (e.g., The trick is performed on stage).
Past Passive is formed using Subject + was/were + past participle (e.g., The spectator was pulled into the boat).
Use the preposition 'by' only when the agent performing the action is important to the meaning of the sentence.
Extreme adjectives like 'freezing' or 'hilarious' do not normally take 'very'; instead, they are modified by 'absolutely'.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often translate sentences literally from their native language and forget that the passive subject receives the action rather than performs it.
commonTrap.wrong: The magic trick performed by the magician every night.
commonTrap.correct: The magic trick is performed by the magician every night.

content.passageTitle: Magic and Illusions: How Do They Do It?
paragraphs: Magic shows have entertained audiences for centuries, but the way modern illusions are produced has changed dramatically. When a thrilling show is performed on a large stage, every single detail is carefully planned months in advance. Special equipment is tested repeatedly, and lights are adjusted to ensure the audience sees only what the illusionist wants them to see. Nothing is left to chance.

One of the most famous street magicians, Dynamo, once amazed millions when he walked across the River Thames. The freezing water was watched by hundreds of confused spectators standing on the bridge. Newspapers later reported how the secret platform was built just beneath the surface. Although the trick was kept hidden for weeks, the fascinating truth was eventually revealed by television producers.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Uncovering The Tattoo Secret

content.summary: Focus on listening for informal reactions and surprise in natural dialogue. Notice how speakers use passive voice structures when talking about things done by professionals, and pay attention to fast connected speech features like elision and linking sounds.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about surprise body art and personal choices.
Identify details such as reactions, opinions, and who performed the action using passive structures.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during fast, casual teenage conversations.

keyPhrases.phrase: Are you out of your mind?
keyPhrases.note: Used to express complete disbelief or shock at someone's foolish action.

keyPhrases.phrase: Where did you get that done?
keyPhrases.note: Used to ask where a professional service like a tattoo or haircut was performed.
Used with the causative structure to show a service was done by someone else.
Used to tell someone to speak more quietly so others do not hear.

connectedSpeech.note: The auxiliary did and pronoun you blend together into a single palatal sound.
The final /t/ in got links directly to the vowel sound in it.
The preposition of weakens to a schwa sound followed by a v.
The /d/ sound links smoothly to the starting vowel of the word it.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Process and Passive Voice

content.summary: Master the passive voice in present and past tenses to describe processes, procedures, and events where the action receiver takes priority over the actor.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Passive Structure
blueprintItems.example: The magic trick is performed on stage every evening.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Past Passive Structure
blueprintItems.example: The missing necklace was found hidden behind the bookshelf.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Service Causative Structure
blueprintItems.example: She had her passport renewed before booking the flight.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the preposition 'by' only when the identity of the agent adds vital information to the sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The report was written yesterday by someone.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The report was written yesterday by the lead investigator.
mechanicsRules.why: Vague agents like someone or anybody make passive sentences weak and unnecessary.

mechanicsRules.rule: Ensure correct subject-verb agreement in the passive voice based on the new grammatical subject.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The documents was signed and mailed this morning.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The documents were signed and mailed this morning.
mechanicsRules.why: The plural subject documents requires the plural auxiliary verb were.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first word of every sentence and all proper nouns including names of people and specific places.
mechanicsRules.badExample: the artifact was discovered in london by professor smith.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The artifact was discovered in London by Professor Smith.
mechanicsRules.why: Proper nouns and sentence beginnings must always start with capital letters in English.

guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences explaining how a common item, such as chocolate or paper, is made using the present passive voice.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following active sentence into the present passive voice:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Workers assemble smartphones in the factory.
targetAnswers: Smartphones are assembled in the factory.
Smartphones are assembled in the factory by workers.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In present passive, use the plural subject followed by 'are' and the past participle 'assembled'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following active sentence into the past passive voice:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Police arrested the suspect near the station.
targetAnswers: The suspect was arrested near the station.
The suspect was arrested near the station by police.
practicumQuestions.explanation: With a singular subject in the past tense, use 'was' plus the past participle 'arrested'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the causative structure 'have something done':
practicumQuestions.promptText: A mechanic repaired my car yesterday.
targetAnswers: I had my car repaired yesterday.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The causative structure is Subject + had + object + past participle (I had my car repaired).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the passive sentence with the correct auxiliary verb:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The letters ______ delivered every morning before noon.
practicumQuestions.hint: Consider if 'letters' is singular or plural.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Letters is plural, so it requires the present auxiliary verb 'are' in the passive voice.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Identify and correct all errors in capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: the museum exhibit was visited by thousands in london.
practicumQuestions.hint: Check the first letter and proper nouns.
targetAnswers: The museum exhibit was visited by thousands in London.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The sentence must begin with a capital 'T', and 'London' must be capitalized as a proper noun.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform this active sentence into the present perfect passive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: They have cancelled the flight due to bad weather.
targetAnswers: The flight has been cancelled due to bad weather.
The flight has been canceled due to bad weather.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Present perfect passive uses 'has/have been' plus the past participle ('cancelled' or 'canceled').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a passive sentence in the past tense using these elements: [The painting / steal / from the gallery].
targetAnswers: The painting was stolen from the gallery.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The correct past passive form uses 'was' and the irregular past participle 'stolen'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this negative active sentence into a passive sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: They do not produce these shoes in Italy.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'These shoes'. Use 'are not produced'.
targetAnswers: These shoes are not produced in Italy.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Negative present passive is formed with 'are not' plus the past participle 'produced'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to show that someone else performed the service:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She will cut her hair tomorrow.
targetAnswers: She will have her hair cut tomorrow.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Future causative uses 'will have' + object + past participle.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a present passive sentence explaining what happens to recyclable plastic:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Plastic bottles / recycle / into new products.
targetAnswers: Plastic bottles are recycled into new products.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Plural subject 'Plastic bottles' takes 'are' and regular past participle 'recycled'.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: How Do They Do It

content.summary: Master the spoken articulation of passive voice structures in present and past tenses. Focus on weak forms of auxiliary verbs such as 'is', 'are', 'was', and 'were', and place primary stress on the main past participle. Clear stress placement ensures listeners understand which actions are performed or received.
content.audioGuidance: When speaking the passive voice, de-emphasize the auxiliary verb. Say 'The trick /wəz/ performed in London' rather than stressing 'was'. Emphasize the lexical verb and the agent when relevant.

pillars.name: Auxiliary Reduction
pillars.explanation: Auxiliary verbs like 'is', 'are', 'was', and 'were' are normally unstressed in connected speech. Pronounce them with schwa sounds to maintain natural speech rhythm.

pillars.name: Past Participle Clarity
pillars.explanation: Ensure past participle endings such as /t/, /d/, or /ɪd/ are articulated clearly before consonant clusters in passive constructions.

pillars.name: Intonation in Explanations
pillars.explanation: Use falling intonation when describing completed manufacturing or production steps in passive voice to signal the end of a clause.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress shifts from the second syllable in illusion to the third syllable in illusionist.
The stress remains on the second syllable for both the verb and the noun form.
The main stress stays on the second syllable across the verb and adjective forms.
The stress shifts from the first syllable in the verb to the third syllable in the adjective.

drills.hint: Pronounce the final /d/ in amazed clearly before spectators.

drills.targetText: The freezing water was stepped onto by the brave illusionist.

drills.focus: Past passive plural 'were' and multisyllabic adjective 'fascinating'
drills.hint: Pronounce 'were' as /wɜː/ and stress the first syllable of 'every'.
